What is causing the F-18, F-22, and F-35 hypoxia issues?

In the F-22's case, when it was first released it relied on an onboard oxygen generation system (OBOGS). Between bugs in that system, problems with the F-22's G-suit, and some of the hose/valve hardware, there were a variety of problems that caused insufficient oxygen flow to the pilot. Since then, a backup oxygen system was weasel worked into the cockpit somewhere -- originally it was left out due to space constraints.

In the F-35's case, who knows. That thing is the next Comanche and the sooner we kill it and use purpose-designed aircraft that are 15x cheaper (or more in many cases), the better, for all of us paying taxes.

In the F-18's case, the earlier models seem to have had cabin pressure issues, while the E/F variants had...you guessed it, OBOGS. Building a complicated system as a backup isn't really a great idea, even if it saves weight.

The F-22 had 2 different issues with their oxygen system. The one caused the crash of that Elmendorf AFB plane in Alaska. The system detected a fire and shut down and the pilot slammed the jet into the terrain trying to twist around and turn his emergency system on. The other issue was the hypoxia and "Raptor cough." The Air Force told us both issues were resolved, but that seems unlikely now.
